name: Double outlet right ventricle
aliases: origin of both great arteries from the right ventricle

reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Both great arteries arise wholly or predominantly from the right ventricle, and a ventricular septal defect is almost always the only outlet of the left ventricle
The clinical picture is determined by the position of the ventricular septal defect relative to the great arteries and by the presence of pulmonary stenosis
A subaortic defect without pulmonary stenosis behaves like a large ventricular septal defect with heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation
A subaortic defect with pulmonary stenosis mimics tetralogy of Fallot with cyanosis
A subpulmonary defect (Taussig-Bing anomaly) directs left ventricular blood to the pulmonary artery and behaves like transposition with cyanosis
A wide anatomical spectrum means individualised surgical planning is essential, guided by defect location and great-artery relationships
Repair aims to baffle the left ventricle to the aorta and relieve any outflow obstruction, sometimes requiring an arterial switch
reference.pathophysiology: Double outlet right ventricle is a conotruncal anomaly in which both great arteries connect entirely or mostly to the morphological right ventricle, so the left ventricle can eject only through a ventricular septal defect. The haemodynamics depend on how the defect relates to the great vessels and whether pulmonary outflow is obstructed. When the defect lies beneath the aorta, oxygenated blood streams preferentially to the aorta and the physiology resembles a simple ventricular septal defect, or tetralogy if pulmonary stenosis coexists. When the defect lies beneath the pulmonary artery, oxygenated left ventricular blood is directed into the pulmonary circulation while systemic output is relatively desaturated, producing a transposition-like picture with cyanosis. The balance of pulmonary and systemic flow and the presence of outflow obstruction thus govern cyanosis and heart failure.
additionalDifferentials: Transposition of the great arteries with ventricular septal defect
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to define the great-artery origins, ventricular septal defect position and outflow obstruction
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to clarify spatial relationships for surgical planning
Cardiac catheterisation to assess pulmonary vascular resistance when needed
Chest radiograph for pulmonary vascularity and cardiac size
Assessment for associated conotruncal and chromosomal anomalies
redFlags: Severe cyanosis in a subpulmonary defect with transposition-like streaming
Heart failure from unobstructed pulmonary overcirculation
Progressive pulmonary vascular disease from a long-standing large shunt
Duct-dependent circulation with critical outflow obstruction
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely with anatomy; favourable subtypes have good results after biventricular repair, while complex forms with remote defects or straddling valves may require single-ventricle palliation and carry a more guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Assuming a fixed physiology when the picture depends heavily on defect location and pulmonary stenosis
Failing to recognise the Taussig-Bing subtype and its transposition-like cyanosis
Underestimating pulmonary vascular disease in an unobstructed large-shunt lesion
Neglecting to screen for associated chromosomal and conotruncal anomalies
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Definitive management is individualised surgical repair guided by ventricular septal defect position and great-artery relationships, typically an intraventricular baffle tunnelling the left ventricle to the aorta, with an arterial switch added for the Taussig-Bing subpulmonary type
Complex anatomy with remote defects or straddling atrioventricular valves may instead require staged single-ventricle palliation culminating in a Fontan circulation
In duct-dependent circulations maintain ductal patency with a prostaglandin infusion pending definitive assessment and surgery
Control pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure medically, using pulmonary artery banding as an interim measure where early complete repair is not feasible
Assess pulmonary vascular resistance by cardiac catheterisation before committing to biventricular repair, as fixed pulmonary hypertension may preclude it
Manage lifelong within a congenital cardiology and cardiac surgical service, monitoring for residual lesions, arrhythmia and baffle or conduit obstruction
Offer screening for associated conotruncal and chromosomal anomalies such as a 22q11 deletion, with genetic counselling for the family
